task: This is a synthetic writing exercise. Using these fictional reporting notes, write a newspaper reported feature for general readers. Draw only on the supplied notes; do not invent additional reported events, scenes, or quotations. Write from this reporting snapshot as of September 9, 2024. Include a headline. Target 450 to 650 words. Follow AP style.

facts.text: The Colton River Dam, built in 1961, supplies water to 220,000 people in the Ridgeline region; it received a Level 2 structural concern designation from federal dam safety engineers in 2023 and has not yet received a fully funded remediation plan.
Bernard Cho, 77, was one of the Colton Dam's original design engineers; now retired, he has followed its deterioration with what he describes as professional regret.

Cho said: "We designed that dam to last 50 years with proper maintenance. It's lasted 63 and the maintenance has been adequate but not comprehensive. I don't know whether to take credit for the engineering or responsibility for what comes next."
Leah Petrov, 41, is a dam safety engineer at the Ridgeline Water District who has spent three years documenting the concrete deterioration in the Colton Dam's upstream face.

Petrov said the concrete's alkali-silica reaction has accelerated since 2018, coinciding with warmer average summer temperatures: "We're seeing expansion rates we didn't see in the first two decades of monitoring. We have less time than the original projections said."
Federal dam safety records show the Colton Dam's downstream inundation zone includes 38,000 residents in three communities.

Ridgeline Water District has applied for $180 million in federal dam rehabilitation funding; the program received $300 million nationally for a priority list of more than 60 structures, and Colton is not yet in the top tier.
Petrov said the funding gap means the district is doing what it can with operating revenues: "We are buying time. We know that. It's not a comfortable thing to know."
Cho reviewed Petrov's monitoring reports at her request; he said the data is consistent with what he would have predicted, and worse than he hoped.

Cho said: "In 1961, we thought we were building something permanent. We weren't, of course. Nothing is. But we built it to last long enough that someone else would have to figure out what to do with it."

The district's emergency action plan was last updated in 2019 and covers evacuation routes for the three downstream communities; Petrov said the plan is technically current but the community notification system it relies on has not been tested recently.

Petrov said she has not shared the full scope of the monitoring data publicly because the district is concerned about property value impacts and community alarm, a decision she described as difficult.

A water policy researcher at Ridgeline University, Dr. Grace Mbeki, said the tension between informing communities and managing alarm is common for infrastructure with slow-developing risks: transparency is required under the district's own public information charter but is practically constrained by who controls the release of raw monitoring data.
The three downstream communities have no designated emergency shelters within their boundaries; residents would need to travel 14 to 22 miles to reach designated safe zones.
Cho said he visits the dam once a year: "Old habit. I like to see it holding. This year it was holding. Next year, I expect it will still be holding. The year after, I don't know."

Petrov said her team's internal estimate is that the dam could be maintained safely for another 12 to 15 years under an accelerated repair program, or six to eight years without one; neither estimate has been formally submitted to federal regulators.
The district's board voted in August 2024 to prioritize the federal funding application and explore bonding options if federal money is not available in time.

Petrov said the most frustrating part of her job is that she can quantify the problem but not the decision: "I can tell you the concrete is losing 2.8 millimeters a year. I cannot tell you who decides when that number becomes an emergency."
Cho said he wrote to the district twice in the past decade to offer his knowledge of the original design drawings; he received no response to either letter until Petrov contacted him directly.

Petrov said Cho's design records provided detail about the original reinforcement spacing that updated drawings did not capture: "He knew things about this dam that weren't in the files. That matters."
